plain_language_summary: Proteins found in many plant foods and birch pollen. In some people, an immune system primed by birch pollen also reacts to similar proteins in raw fruits and vegetables.
what_it_does: These proteins are part of the plant’s defence system.
typical_sources: Birch pollen; apple, peach, cherry, celery, peanut and some other plant foods
example_allergens: Bet v 1 (birch pollen); Mal d 1 (apple); Ara h 8 (peanut)
why_it_can_matter: They often cause itching or tingling in the mouth after raw fruit, sometimes called pollen-food allergy syndrome or oral allergy syndrome.
heat_and_digestion: Usually weakened by cooking and digestion, so some people tolerate cooked versions better. This is not guaranteed for everyone.
cross_reactivity_note: Related PR-10 proteins in birch pollen and plant foods can cross-react.

plain_language_summary: Very common proteins inside plant cells. They are found in many pollens, fruits, vegetables and legumes.
what_it_does: They help plant cells change shape and grow.
typical_sources: Grass, birch and weed pollens; apple, peach, celery, peanut, soy and other plant foods
example_allergens: Bet v 2 (birch pollen); Mal d 4 (apple); Ara h 5 (peanut)
why_it_can_matter: Because profilins are similar across many plants, some people sensitised through pollen may react to several plant foods.
heat_and_digestion: Often weakened by digestion; cooking may also reduce activity, but responses vary.
cross_reactivity_note: Profilins are considered pan-allergens: similar forms occur in many pollens and plant foods.

plain_language_summary: Small, tough plant proteins that move fatty molecules within the plant. They are common in fruits, nuts and seeds.
what_it_does: They bind and transport lipids and help protect plants.
typical_sources: Peach, apple, walnut, peanut, and some other fruits, nuts and seeds
example_allergens: Pru p 3 (peach); Mal d 3 (apple); Ara h 9 (peanut)
why_it_can_matter: They can sometimes cause more widespread reactions than the pollen-related fruit proteins, and reactions may occur with processed foods.
heat_and_digestion: Often resist heat and digestion, so cooking does not reliably make them harmless.
cross_reactivity_note: Different nsLTPs in fruits and nuts can cross-react, especially in some geographic regions.

plain_language_summary: Large storage proteins that help seeds grow. They are important allergens in peanuts, soybeans and some tree nuts.
what_it_does: They store nutrients for the developing plant.
typical_sources: Peanut, soybean, many tree nuts and seeds
example_allergens: Ara h 1 and Ara h 3 (peanut); Gly m 5 and Gly m 6 (soybean)
why_it_can_matter: These are major food-allergen proteins and may be involved in more severe reactions in some people.
heat_and_digestion: Many cupins are relatively stable during cooking and digestion.
cross_reactivity_note: Some cupins from related legumes and nuts can cross-react, but clinical relevance varies.

plain_language_summary: Small seed-storage proteins found in peanuts, tree nuts and seeds. Some are major allergy triggers.
what_it_does: They store amino acids and other nutrients for the seed.
typical_sources: Peanut, tree nuts, sesame, mustard and some other seeds
example_allergens: Ara h 2 and Ara h 6 (peanut); Ana o 3 (cashew); Ses i 1 (sesame)
why_it_can_matter: They are among the important peanut, nut and seed allergens and have been associated with severe reactions in some people.
cross_reactivity_note: Some 2S albumins from different nuts and seeds can cross-react, but this is highly individual.

plain_language_summary: Proteins that coat tiny oil droplets inside oily seeds and nuts.
what_it_does: They stabilise the seed’s oil bodies.
typical_sources: Peanut, sesame, hazelnut and other oil-rich seeds
example_allergens: Ara h 10, Ara h 11, Ara h 14 and Ara h 15 (peanut); Ses i 4 and Ses i 5 (sesame)
why_it_can_matter: They may be relevant for some people with seed or nut allergy, although they are less well characterised than major allergens such as Ara h 2.
heat_and_digestion: Their behaviour during digestion and processing is still being studied.
cross_reactivity_note: Cross-reactivity is not yet well defined for most oleosins.

plain_language_summary: Proteins that plants use as a natural defence. They can block enzymes that break down proteins in the gut.
what_it_does: They inhibit digestive enzymes such as trypsin and chymotrypsin.
typical_sources: Soybean, peanut and other legumes and seeds
example_allergens: Gly m TI / Kunitz trypsin inhibitor (soybean); some peanut protease inhibitors
why_it_can_matter: Some people with legume or seed allergy may have immune responses to these proteins, but their clinical importance varies by food and person.
heat_and_digestion: Some protease inhibitors can remain active after processing, although heating and fermentation can reduce activity in foods.
cross_reactivity_note: Cross-reactivity is not well established and should not be assumed.

plain_language_summary: Muscle proteins found in shellfish, insects and other invertebrates. They are a major cause of shellfish allergy.
typical_sources: Shrimp, crab, lobster and other shellfish; dust mites and cockroaches contain related proteins
why_it_can_matter: Tropomyosin allergy can cause food reactions and may overlap with sensitivity to dust-mite or cockroach proteins.
cross_reactivity_note: Tropomyosins are pan-allergens across shellfish, insects and mites; cross-reactivity can be clinically important.

plain_language_summary: The main family of proteins in cow’s milk. They form curds when milk is used to make cheese.
what_it_does: They provide nutrients and help carry calcium and phosphate.
typical_sources: Cow’s milk and products made from it
example_allergens: Bos d 8 / caseins, including alpha-, beta- and kappa-casein
why_it_can_matter: Caseins are major milk-allergy proteins and can be relevant in both mild and severe milk allergy.
heat_and_digestion: They are generally relatively heat-stable, so baked-milk tolerance is individual and must be medically assessed.
cross_reactivity_note: Caseins from cow, goat and sheep milk are closely related, so cross-reactivity is common.

plain_language_summary: Proteins in egg white; several can trigger egg allergy. Ovalbumin is the most abundant, while ovomucoid is often more heat-stable.
what_it_does: They provide nutrients and protection for the developing embryo.
why_it_can_matter: Egg-white proteins are common causes of IgE-mediated egg allergy, especially in children.
heat_and_digestion: Ovalbumin is more easily changed by heat than ovomucoid; some people tolerate baked egg, but this must be assessed by a clinician.
cross_reactivity_note: Cross-reactivity between hen, duck and other bird eggs can occur.
